claim: Human cancer is driven by the acquisition of mutations in cells of somatic origin.
source: Human cancer is driven by the acquisition of mutations in cells of somatic origin.
evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge about cancer etiology.

claim: Somatic mutations comprise several distinct classes of DNA sequence changes, including single-nucleotide substitutions, small insertions and deletions (indels), copy number alterations, and structural rearrangements.
source: Somatic mutations comprise several distinct classes of DNA sequence changes, including single-nucleotide substitutions, small insertions and deletions (indels), copy number alterations, and structural rearrangements (Weir et al., 2007; Chin and Gray, 2008; Stratton et al., 2009; Pleasance et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing types of somatic mutations.

claim: Driver mutations are genetic variations that are directly involved in cancer development.
source: Somatic mutations can be further characterized based on their oncogenic ability: genetic variations that are directly involved in cancer development are termed "driver" mutations, whereas mutations that do not confer any obvious advantage are referred to as "passenger" mutations (Davies et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Davies et al., 2005.

claim: Passenger mutations are mutations that do not confer any obvious advantage.
source: Somatic mutations can be further characterized based on their oncogenic ability: genetic variations that are directly involved in cancer development are termed "driver" mutations, whereas mutations that do not confer any obvious advantage are referred to as "passenger" mutations (Davies et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to Davies et al., 2005.

claim: Genetic changes in somatic cells arise as a result of defective DNA repair mechanisms and/or imprecise DNA replication.
source: In all cases, genetic changes in somatic cells arise as a result of defective DNA repair mechanisms and/or imprecise DNA replication, and can develop spontaneously, be acquired over the lifetime of an individual, or by direct exposure to mutagens, such as tobacco smoke and ionizing UV radiation (Pfeifer, 2010; Pleasance et al., 2010; Helleday et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to studies on DNA damage and repair mechanisms.

claim: Genetic changes in somatic cells can develop spontaneously, be acquired over the lifetime of an individual, or by direct exposure to mutagens, such as tobacco smoke and ionizing UV radiation.
